passage:
In the Accra school corridor, Paulo held out his phone to Kwame. "Look. I wasn't going to show you, but you should know."
The screen showed a new group chat called "no Kwame". Someone from his class had shared screenshots of Kwame's messages from the class chat, with jokes underneath. Kwame read a line about his football boots and felt his ears go hot. Names he knew, people he had sat with at lunch.
"Thank you for telling me," Kwame said, voice low. He did not go into the class chat. At lunch he went straight to Mr Boateng, the form teacher, and said, "Something happened. Can I show you?"

qa.q: What was the new group chat called?
qa.a: The new group chat was called "no Kwame".

qa.q: What was Kwame feeling as he read the screenshots and the jokes underneath?
qa.a: Kwame felt hurt and embarrassed. The hot ears and low voice show how it stung to see people laughing behind his back.

qa.q: What did Kwame choose to do instead of answering in the class chat?
qa.a: Kwame thanked Paulo and went to his form teacher, Mr Boateng, and asked to show what had happened. Telling a trusted adult kept things from getting worse.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Paulo to show Kwame the phone?
qa.a: Paulo was probably nervous but caring, since Paulo said "you should know". Showing something painful took courage and trust in Kwame.

grounding: A teenager learns that people from their class made another group chat without them and shared screenshots of their messages, and goes to a trusted adult.

passage:
The school counsellor's room smelled of orange peel. Sahil sat with a hood up, phone face down on the chair arm.
"Salma showed me this at break," Sahil said at last. The screen showed a chat Sahil had never been added to, and screenshots of Sahil's own messages, a voice note transcribed with joke captions.
"Thank you for showing me," the counsellor said. "That sounds painful, being talked about behind your back. It is not your fault." They asked Sahil whether they could take the phone to the head of pastoral care together, that same afternoon.
Sahil nodded, and the hood came down slowly.

qa.q: What did Sahil's hood do at the end of the scene?
qa.a: The hood came down slowly.

qa.q: What might Sahil have been feeling while sitting with a hood up and the phone face down?
qa.a: Sahil was probably hurt and ashamed, shutting out the room with the hood and the face-down phone. It is painful to see one's own messages made into jokes.

qa.q: What did the counsellor do that helped Sahil?
qa.a: The counsellor thanked Sahil for showing the phone, said it was not Sahil's fault, and offered to take it to the head of pastoral care that afternoon. Sahil was not left alone with it.

qa.q: What might Salma have been thinking when showing Sahil the chat at break?
qa.a: Salma probably felt worried for Sahil and thought Sahil should know. Showing it was a caring step, even though it was hard to do.

grounding: A teenager finds that people from their class made another chat without them and shared screenshots of their messages, and a school counsellor responds the same day.

passage:
Wednesday
Kishore sent me a screenshot at lunch. It's from a group called "10B real". I'm not in it. Nearly everyone else is.
The screenshot was of MY message from our class group, about the science project, with circles drawn around my spelling mistake and a line underneath: "Aparna the professor strikes again."
I read it in the bathroom, again and again. My face felt like it was burning. So all this time they've been making fun of me in a place I can't even see.
When I got home I didn't eat. Amma came and sat on my bed and asked what happened. I showed her. She didn't get angry at me or say "ignore it". She said, "This is not your fault, Aparna. You didn't do anything wrong." She held my hand while I cried.
Then she wrote an email to Mrs Pillai, the class teacher, with me beside her, and sent it tonight. Tomorrow she's coming to school with me.

qa.q: What was the other group called?
qa.a: The group was called "10B real".

qa.q: What was Aparna feeling after seeing the screenshot?
qa.a: Aparna felt humiliated and deeply hurt, with a burning face, realising classmates had been mocking Aparna somewhere out of sight.

qa.q: How did Amma support Aparna well?
qa.a: Amma sat with Aparna, listened, said it was not Aparna's fault, and emailed the class teacher that same night with Aparna beside her.

qa.q: How might Kishore have felt sending the screenshot?
qa.a: Kishore was probably worried and uneasy, wanting Aparna to know but perhaps unsure whether it would hurt Aparna more.

grounding: A teenager discovers a class chat made without them that shares screenshots of their messages, and the exclusion stings deeply.

passage:
In the kasba school, the Class 9 chat was where Bhupen asked about homework and shared cricket scores. So when Nitin showed him a second group, "9B boys only", with Bhupen missing from the member list, it felt like a slap.
There were screenshots of his messages. His "sir, please tell answer of Q5" was pasted with laughing faces, and someone had written, "our little topper again."
Bhupen said nothing on the walk home past the sugarcane field. He didn't eat much at dinner either. His mother noticed.
"Something happened, beta?"
He handed her the phone. She scrolled slowly, then put her arm around him. "You asked a question. That's what school is for. This is not your fault."
She called his class teacher, Yadav sir, that same night. Bhupen listened from the doorway as she spoke calmly and firmly. Yadav sir said he would speak to the class tomorrow.

qa.q: Which group was Bhupen missing from?
qa.a: Bhupen was missing from the group called "9B boys only".

qa.q: What does Bhupen's silence on the walk home suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt hurt and ashamed, stung by being left out and mocked behind his back.

qa.q: How did Bhupen's mother respond, and why did it help?
qa.a: She noticed he was quiet, listened, told him it was not his fault, and called his class teacher that same night; that same-day response made Bhupen feel protected.

qa.q: How might Nitin have felt showing Bhupen the group?
qa.a: Nitin probably felt uneasy and loyal, not wanting his friend mocked in secret but knowing it would hurt.

grounding: A teenager sees screenshots of his messages mocked in a group made without him, and the exclusion stings deeply.

passage: In Melbourne, on Thursday, Jamal hung back after science and held out his phone, looking uneasy. "I don't think this is okay. You should see it." It was a second group, "Year 10 real", with everyone from the old chat except Mei. Pinned at the top were screenshots of Mei's messages, her long one about the history project and her question about the formal, each with a row of laughing faces underneath. Mei's ears went hot. She handed the phone back and said, "Cool. Whatever." On the tram home she stared out the window with no music on. At dinner her dad noticed she wasn't eating and asked gently what was wrong. She showed him the screenshots Jamal had sent her. He sat beside her, said it was not her fault and that being talked about like that really hurts, and they emailed her year coordinator together. A reply came before nine: the coordinator would meet Mei first thing tomorrow.

qa.q: What was the second group called?
qa.a: It was called "Year 10 real".

qa.q: What does Mei's "Cool. Whatever." suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt deeply hurt and humiliated but was trying to hide it in front of Jamal.

qa.q: How did Mei's dad support her that evening?
qa.a: He sat beside her, said it was not her fault and that it really hurts, and emailed the year coordinator with her that same evening.

qa.q: Why might Jamal have looked uneasy when he showed Mei the group?
qa.a: Jamal was likely torn: he did not want to upset Mei, but he felt the group was wrong and that she deserved to know.

grounding: Shows a teenager discovering a group chat made without her where her messages are screenshotted and mocked, and how much being discussed behind her back stings.
